title: SC3 ABRF R Workshop
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the SC3 ABRF R Workshop. This 4-hour course is designed to take you through the fundamentals of R in a core facility context.

title: SC3 ABRF R Workshop
text:
Schedule

35 minutes: Module 1 - The Modern R Ecosystem & Project Sandbox
35 minutes: Module 2 - R Syntax & Core Data Structures
50 minutes: Module 3 - Core Admin - Wrangling & Visualizing iLab Revenue
45 minutes: Module 4 - Core Operations - Instrument QA/QC & Analytics

title: SC3 ABRF R Workshop
text:
Prerequisites
Please ensure you have the following installed before we begin: 1. R (version 4.2.0 or higher) 2. Positron 3. The tidyverse package
You can install the required packages by running the following in your R console:
install.packages("tidyverse")

title: 2  The Modern R Ecosystem & Project Sandbox
text:
2.1 Introduction to R
Download this Notebook (R-Introductions.qmd)
The R programming language is an incredible, open-source data analysis language used by many researchers globally to quickly to compute, analyze, and visualize their data. The beauty of R is the massive community-driven repositories of programs that enable everyone, even users new to R, the ability to immediately begin performing simple to complex analyses. From simple plotting of facility revenue to complex machine-learning analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing. This workshop is broken down into 4 modules covering how to set-up R, learn R basic syntax (i.e. how R code is written), how to plot core facility revenue with data exported from iLab, and finally how to perform QA/QC analyses of instrument metadata to identify bottlenecks in the lab. Module 1 will focus on a gentle introdution to R and how to setup our IDE.
Goals for this module:

title: 2  The Modern R Ecosystem & Project Sandbox
text:
Understand the difference between base and virtual R ennvironments
Learn how to install R packages
Comprehend where to find R packages CRAN, Bioconductor, etc.


2.1.1 Positron IDE & R Basics
Before we can get into processing data, we first need to learn the basics of our compute environment. For this workshop this will be you laptop, later though this could be a remote desktop, server, or even the cloud depending on your institutional rescources.
To begin, we will need to install R and an IDE. IDE stands for Interactive Development Environment, and is our homebase for interacting and using the R programing language. For this workshop we will be using the Positron IDE, an IDE made by the company Posit. It replaced RStudio the original IDE for R. It comes with some additional bells and whistles we won’t be getting into in this workshop, but are highly useful if you continue your journey in using R. It’s forked from Microsoft’s Visual Studio Code, and if you have used VS Code before you will notice the striking similarities.
Posit has released an entire series on how to use and get familiar with Positron IDE which you can find on their website here. You can use these to refresh yourself after this workshop. For now though, follow along on the presentation screen.


2.1.2 Reproducibility Crisis & How to Fix It (Virtual Environments)
How many times have you heard, “Look at my lab notebook for the protocol and it will work.”, to only find out that, no, it in fact does not work. Either due to a missing step, wrong concentrations, incorrect buffer, etc. In informatics, we face a similar reproducibility crisis, but instead of a difference in buffer components, its program versions. Pacakages in R are often created by scientists and researchers to address a very specific issue. After publication, if the program is used by many others, it often receives routine updates. Depending on its popularity, these updates could be weekly to annually. Some updates just fix bugs or errors with the code, while others may change how the program itself works and how we use it. To avoid version issues when sharing code or having someone else run code that we wrote, we use a version managing tool to lock versions of softwares we are using. This especially helps to prevent those pesky IT/TS departments forced updates on our computers that would otherwise break everything.
In R, this tool is called renv, which stands for R environment. This is a virtual ennvirment management tool that will help us as we will see later. When you installed R on your computer, it created a base R environment where all the files and code to use R are located. This base environment is accessible to everything and everyone on your computer. In contrast virtual enrivonments are locations on your computer only accessible who and what you allow. This is typically a location or folder you chose each time your create one. For this workshop we will begin by creating a virtual ennvironment in the folder we are currently in. We can do this by using the renv package below:
# First we need to install renv using the install.packages() function
install.packages("renv")

# Next we activate our virtual enrivonment with the activate() function
renv::activate()
Next, we will install one of the most invaluable packages within the R ecosystem tidyverse. tidyverse is a compilation of various data handling, transformation, processing, and visualization R packages wrapped into a single package. This makes for easier install and loading, and it will handle the majority of what we are going to cover in this workshop. To install tidyverse copy and paste the code below in your R console:
# install the tidyverse package from CRAN
install.packages("tidyverse")
Now, we are ready to begin to write our first R program!

title: 3  R Syntax & Core Data Structures
text:
3.1.1 Hello, world!
In all seriousness though, coding can be as simple or complex as you make it. For instance, we are going to begin by writing the first program everyone learns in any programming langueage, printing the Hello, world! statement. We will use the print() function from base R. We will go over each part of it shortly. Begin, typing the following in your R script:

print("Hello, world!")

[1] "Hello, world!"


As you can see the statement “Hello, world!” was output (or printed, hence the function name) below in our R console. We called the print() function which takes as input a string (text), number, or even a variable as input. This print() function is used a lot across many programming langueages. You have commonly encountered it in your day-to-day jobs. When coding it is often used to print a status update, error message, warning, etc. to the user as feedback so we aren’t just starting at a static screen wondering if something has happened or we have messed up.
Now we are going to add a layer to our print() code from earlier. What if we wanted to store a message to ourselves, say remember to drink our coffee while it is still hot, and view it later. We achieve this by creating a vairable and casting (storing) a value in it using the <- operator.

1note <- "Remember, to drink your coffee, while it is hot!"
print("Here we are going to print our note below:")
2print(note)


1

this line stores our message about our coffee into the vaiable “note”.

2

then we print it to stdout.




[1] "Here we are going to print our note below:"
[1] "Remember, to drink your coffee, while it is hot!"


Congrats! You have learned two basics in the R programming language, how to call a function print, and how to store a variable with the <- operator. Now we are going to move on to store data in R.


3.1.2 Vector, the simplest way to store multiple data
Above we stored our first data, a single string into the variable note. But what if we wanted to store a a list of numbers? In R, a series of data is called a vector (in R we also have list objects, which behave differently but can look similar). We begin a vector using the c() and separating elements in the vector with a comma. Below, let’s create a vector of numbers 1-5.

num_vec <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
print(num_vec)

[1] 1 2 3 4 5


As you can see, we stored a list of the numbers 1-5 in the variable called num_vec. Unlike before, our variable now stored as numbers, specifically as integers. You’ll notice how we dropped the "" marks as we intended to store numbers instead of strings.
However we can mix data types in vectors, lets see what happends when we try to mix numbers and strings:

mix_vec <- c(1, "the", 2, "cow", 3, "moos")
print(mix_vec)

[1] "1"    "the"  "2"    "cow"  "3"    "moos"




3.1.3 DataFrames: R’s Excel Table Data Object
Vetors are very useful and a core object type in R. Many other useful objects are built on top of vectors. However, the most common type of data we deal with in R will be DataFrames/Tibbles. DataFrames (or the modern equivalent Tibbles, used in tidyverse) are the R equivalent of tables in Excel.
Tibbles are not included in base R, like Dataframes are, so here we need to attach the tidyverse package we installed earlier.Copy and run the following code to generate a dataframe:

library(tidyverse)


1

Here we use the base R function data.frame() function to create a dataframe object

2

Here we use the tidyverse tibble() function to create a tibble object.




── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

1df <- data.frame(name=c("A", "B"), value = c(5, 10))
print(df)

2tib <- tibble(name=c("C", "D"), value = c(15, 20))
print(tib)

  name value
1    A     5
2    B    10
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  name  value
  <chr> <dbl>
1 C        15
2 D        20


Now we have two separate frames of data. Next we will show you how we can combine them. This is useful if we have multiple datasets we have loaded individually and now need to combine. Here we will use the dplyr function bind_rows().

combined_df <- bind_rows(df, tib)


3.1.3.1 Accessing Data inside Dataframes/Tibbles
Now let’s take a look on how to access rows, columns, and specific values using base R’s indexing methods. First let’s see how we can view the row and column names of a dataframe:

1print(rownames(combined_df))
2print(colnames(combined_df))


1

rownames() returns a vector of the row index names, or numbers if no names are present

2

colnames() returns a vector of the column names, or numbers if no names are present.




[1] "1" "2" "3" "4"
[1] "name"  "value"


Above we can see that, the row indexes are numbers, and our column names are “name” and “value”. We can use the rownames() and colnames() functions to replace the old labels with new onces if we wanted to as well. Next lets see how we print specific rows:

print(combined_df[1,])

  name value
1    A     5

print(combined_df[3,])

  name value
3    C    15


Here the numbers represent coordinates where the x-value corresponds to row number, and the y-value corresponds to a column number within the dataframe. By leaving the second value empty (after the comma) we print a single row. The same would be true if we switched the numbers around, and we would print a column instead. To access specific data, we use both coordinate values:

print(combined_df[1,2])

[1] 5




3.1.3.2 Importing Tabular/CSV Data
Now that we understand the structure of dataframes/tibbles in R, let’s learn how to import our CSV/TSV/Excel-formatted data files as dataframes into R. Here we are going to leverage the the read.csv() from base R. Later we will work on data we pull from iLab, for now please downlaod a sample data set from here. The read.csv() has a few parameters. We can convenitley see a quick help guide on any function of interest by using the ? before any function call try it first below:

?read.csv()
1csv_data <- read.csv("data/fy26_costs.csv")
print(csv_data)

2csv_data$Costs


1

Here we only need to pass the path to our file, in some cases, you may need to specify which colums you would like to keep, and/or skip loading into memory.

2

Here is another way we can print entire columns of a dataframe, by accessing the specific column name of the dataframe with $.

The summary() function take a dataframe or vector as input and quickly output basic statistical analysis of the distribution of the data. You’ll notice that our Month column is a columm filled with strings. Instead we get an overview of the length, number of unique identities, number of blank entries, and the minimum and maximum number of characters in a row. All other columns contain numerical values and so we get quick distribution summaries of our data.
As a final example of what we can do with R combining everything we have gone over in this notebook. Lets print a message telling us the sum total of our costs, sales, and revenue numbers for FY26:

text:
4.3 Data Wrangling with dplyr
In this segment, we process raw billing data from iLab systems. We will clean test accounts, focus on completed/paid transactions, use the standard R native pipe |>, and parse timestamp strings into useful data features (Months and Quarter).

4.3.1 Downloading iLab Data
We are going to download our revenue reports from iLab for FY26. If you do not have access to this information in iLab, please use the data provided here.


4.3.2 Load in iLab Data
Now let’s load in our data as have done previously:

ilab_raw <- read.csv("data/module3_FY26_full.csv", header = TRUE)



4.3.3 Clean iLab Data
We have our iLab data loaded into memory and stored in the vairable ilab_raw. However, if we inspect the data we will notice it is full of n/a, or just empty data points throughout the columns of the dataframe. We need to clean up the data and get it in a state that is useful for reporting an more informative for plotting.
We are going to accomplish this using the dplyr package bundled with tidyverse. Our goals are to: * Filter out internal test accounts (Customer Name != "Test Account"), and unpaid/cancelled invoices (payment_status == "Paid"). * Parse timestamps into Month and Quarter using lubridate functions. * Format date categories cleanly for downstream visualization.

cleaned_revenue_data <- ilab_raw |>
  filter(
    Customer.Name != "Test Account",
    Billing.Status == "billing_initialized"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    date = mdy_hm(Billing.Date),
    month_num = month(date),
    month_label = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    quarter = factor(paste0("Q", quarter(date)))
  ) |>
  arrange(date)

title: 4  Core Admin - Wrangling & Visualizing iLab Revenue
text:
4.4 Visualizing Revenue Trends with ggplot2
Now that our data is clean, we will aggregate revenue trends and build report-ready figures.

4.4.1 Monthly Revenue (Bar Chart)
To identify seasonal dips, we aggregate total revenue by month.

monthly_revenue <- cleaned_revenue_data |> 
  group_by(month_label) |> 
  summarise(total_revenue = sum(Total.Price), .groups = "drop")
head(monthly_revenue)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  month_label total_revenue
  <ord>               <dbl>
1 Jan                37851.
2 Feb                90211 
3 Mar                89684.
4 Apr                71493.
5 May                69307.
6 Jun                53123.



p1 <- ggplot(monthly_revenue, aes(x = month_label, y = total_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "orange", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "$")) +
  labs(
    title="Total Monthly Revenue (FY26)",
    subtitle="Analysis of seasonal dips in core facility billing",
    x="Month",
    y="Revenue (USD)"
  ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title=element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

  p1










4.4.2 Quartely Revenue By Institution Type (Stacked Bar & Line Charts)
Next, we evaluate revenue per quarter broken down by Institution Type (Internal vs. External)

quarterly_institution_revenue <- cleaned_revenue_data |> 
  mutate(Institution.Type = if_else(
    Customer.Institute == "Texas A&M University",
    "Internal",
    "External"
  )) |> 
    group_by(quarter, Institution.Type) |> 
    summarise(total_revenue = sum(Total.Price), .groups = "drop")

  labs(
    title = "Quarterly Revenue Trajectory",
    subtitle = "Comparison of growth trends between Internal and External/Affiliate clients",
    x = "Quarter",
    y = "Revenue (USD)",
    color = "Institution Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p3










4.4.4 Exporint Report-Ready Plots
To export high-resolution figures for reports or internal sharing, we use ggsave().

dir.create("output_plots", showWarnings = FALSE)

ggsave(
  filename = "output_plots/monthly_revenue_trend.pdf",
  plot = p1,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)

ggsave(
  filename = "output_plots/quarterly_revenue_institution_stacked.png",
  plot = p2,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)

ggsave(
  filename = "output_plots/quarterly_revenue_institution_line.jpeg",
  plot = p3,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)
